about: Place names for Dashiell (drafts). Every place template in src/gen/data/places.ts has 6–10 name sets; the engine picks one per place per case. See rules.md for how each form is used and README.md for slots and counts.

slots.{street}: a cross street (or other named street) in the case’s neighbourhood, full name: “Rivington Street”. From streets.json.
slots.{avenue}: a north–south avenue or main street in the case’s neighbourhood, full name with any article it carries: “Tenth Avenue”, “the Bowery”. From streets.json. Never the same street as {street}.
slots.{V}: the family name of the person whose own place this is: the victim’s address in a murder, the owner’s in a lost-item or lost-pet case. Residence sets always carry it; other sets carry it only when marked keeping.
slots.{W}: the family name of the landlady posted at this place (fixture role landlady). Used only on landlady-watched templates.

fields.local: what people in the neighbourhood say (1–3 forms)
fields.short: the notebook grid and the rules; 1–2 words
fields.epithets: descriptive tags, each read after a comma: “Mancuso’s, where the smoke hung over the tables like a second ceiling”
fields.sense: sound, sight, smell: the senses the place is strongest in, strongest first
fields.fits: optional; the neighbourhoods this set may be drawn in (it names a real landmark or a fixed street). Absent means any neighbourhood.
fields.keeping: optional; true means the set names the place as {V}’s own. Drawn only when the place belongs to {V} in this case, and then always one of these.

res-apartment.proper: {V}’s apartment on the fourth floor of the Linden Arms on {street}
epithets: where the mailboxes had lost half their names
with a super in the basement who kept an owl’s hours
four flights up, and every one of them personal

res-apartment.proper: {V}’s four rooms on the fourth floor of the Excelsior, a walk-up on {street}
epithets: which had never once excelled at anything
where the stair light gave up at the third landing
with a front hall no bigger than a coat closet

res-apartment.proper: {V}’s apartment on the fourth floor over Grieco’s fish market on {avenue}
epithets: that smelled faithfully of the fish market four floors down
where the gulls came inland to ask about the fish
with sawdust from the market tracked up every stair

res-apartment.proper: {V}’s flat on the fourth floor of the red-brick house at {street} and {avenue}, the one with the green fire escape
epithets: with its fire escape painted the green of a billiard table
where somebody on the second floor practised the cornet
which leaned a little toward the avenue, as if listening

res-apartment.proper: {V}’s apartment on the fourth floor of the Adelaide on {street}
epithets: where the elevator had been coming soon since 1911
with a stained-glass street door nobody had ever cleaned
whose front steps were the block’s favourite place to sit

res-apartment.proper: {V}’s apartment on the fourth floor over Novak’s bakery on {avenue}
epithets: that smelled of rye bread before anybody was awake to want it
where the floors stayed warm from the ovens below
with flour dust on every banister

res-apartment.proper: {V}’s apartment at the back of the fourth floor of the building on {street} that the block called the Wedding Cake
epithets: with more plaster curlicues than sense
iced in white stone like a cake nobody was allowed to eat
whose cornice dropped a piece of itself on the sidewalk every spring

res-brownstone.proper: {V}’s rooms on the parlour floor of the brownstone on {street} with the stone lions on the stoop
epithets: guarded by two stone lions with no noses left between them
whose stoop had been worn smooth in the middle
with its curtains drawn at noon

res-brownstone.proper: {V}’s rooms in the old Van Tassel house on {street}
epithets: which no Van Tassel had set foot in since the Civil War
with a brass knocker shaped like a fist
where the family portraits had been sold and the nails left in the wall

res-brownstone.proper: {V}’s rooms on the second floor of the brownstone on {street} with the wisteria over the door
epithets: with a wisteria over the door that had opinions about the mail slot
that smelled of wisteria in May and wet stone the rest of the year
where the vine had got into the gutters and was working on the roof

res-brownstone.proper: {V}’s rooms in the brownstone on {street} where old Dr. Pettibone used to set bones
epithets: with the doctor’s brass plate still on the railing
where strangers still knocked at the side door out of habit
which still smelled faintly of iodine

res-brownstone.proper: {V}’s rooms on the parlour floor of the narrow brownstone on {street}, squeezed between a church and a bakery
epithets: twelve feet wide and proud of every one of them
where you could touch both walls of the hall at once
with a church on one side and a bakery on the other, which covered most needs

res-brownstone.proper: {V}’s rooms in the brownstone on {street} with the bay window
epithets: with a bay window sticking out into the street like a chin
where the street could see in and mostly did
with a window seat worn to the shape of whoever sat in it
the last three houses on the block the builders hadn’t bought yet
with a new apartment house glaring at it from across the street
where every stoop had a flower box and every flower box had given up
where the cherry syrup smell climbed the stairs ahead of you
over a window full of hot-water bottles
with a stair so steep it counted as exercise

res-walkup.proper: {V}’s walk-up over the Eagle Drug Store on {street}, the one with the stuffed eagle in the window
epithets: over a stuffed eagle that had seen everything and said nothing
three flights of bare wood with no runner
where the hall bulb burned out about as often as it was changed
over a pharmacy that sold as much wine tonic as aspirin
that smelled of camphor and boiled coffee
where the ceiling fan in the store below hummed up through the floor

res-walkup.proper: {V}’s walk-up over Gottlieb’s drugstore at {street} and {avenue}
epithets: where the soda fountain gurgled up through the floorboards
with a back stair that swayed a little when it had company
over a window advertising a cure for everything but the rent

res-walkup.proper: {V}’s walk-up over Doc Farrow’s drugstore on {street}
epithets: over a druggist the whole block called Doc without ever having seen a diploma
where the hall smelled of liniment and cabbage
with a door that stuck in wet weather and in dry weather too

res-walkup.proper: {V}’s walk-up over the Palace Pharmacy on {avenue}
epithets: over a pharmacy that was no kind of palace
where the electric sign buzzed against the bedroom window all night
up a stair lit by the pharmacy sign and nothing else

res-walkup.proper: {V}’s walk-up over Ostrowski’s drugstore on {street}, three flights up and one room deep
epithets: one room deep and three flights tall, like a filing cabinet somebody lived in
where the roof leaked only on Sundays, out of respect
over a window full of trusses and corn plasters

res-suite.proper: {V}’s suite on the sixth floor of the Hotel Aldine on {street}
epithets: where the rent was by the week and the questions were by appointment
with an elevator that ran when it felt appreciated
whose hall carpet had a path worn down the middle like a cow track

res-suite.proper: {V}’s suite at the Marlowe, a residential hotel on {avenue}
epithets: a hotel for bachelors and people who had stopped explaining
where every hallway smelled of shaving soap
with a lobby fern older than the desk clerk

res-suite.proper: {V}’s two rooms and bath at the Hotel Wentworth on {street}
epithets: two rooms and a bath, and the bath was the proud one
where the house rules were framed on every door and obeyed behind none
with its name in gold leaf on a window nobody washed

res-suite.proper: {V}’s suite on the top floor of the Hotel Castleton on {avenue}, under the copper roof
epithets: under a copper roof gone as green as a pickle
where the top-floor rent came with a view and a draught
which had been fashionable for about a year in 1904

res-suite.proper: {V}’s suite at the St. Ives on {street}, the residential hotel full of retired actors
epithets: where every retired actor in the building took the stairs like an entrance
full of people who had played the Palace once and would tell you about it
with a lobby done up like the set of a play that had closed

res-suite.proper: {V}’s suite at the Hotel Pembroke on {street}, six floors of plain brick
epithets: six floors of brick with nothing to say for itself
where the carpet had been red once and could prove it in the corners
whose one ambition was to be left alone

res-suite.proper: {V}’s suite at the Belmont Residence on {avenue}, over the tearoom
epithets: over a tearoom that sold more gossip than tea
that smelled of toast and floor wax on every landing
where the doormat said WELCOME and the desk clerk didn’t

res-backhouse.proper: {V}’s little house on the back lot behind {street}, the old stable with the hayloft door
epithets: with a hayloft door nobody had opened since the horse moved out
where you could still find a horseshoe nail between the floorboards
down a passage so narrow you went through it sideways

res-backhouse.proper: {V}’s house behind the Weber place on {street}, down the gravel lane
epithets: down a gravel lane that announced every step
which the Webers pretended wasn’t there
with a tin washtub hung by the door like a coat of arms

res-backhouse.proper: {V}’s cottage on the back lot off {street}, with the fig tree
epithets: with a fig tree wrapped in burlap every winter like a patient
that smelled of tomato vines all August
where the lot was more garden than lot

res-backhouse.proper: {V}’s house at the back of the carriage yard on {street}
epithets: at the back of a carriage yard without a carriage in it
reached through an arch with a gate that complained on its hinges
where the cobbles came up to meet your ankles

res-backhouse.proper: {V}’s two-room house behind Rourke’s old saloon on {street}
epithets: behind a saloon that now claimed to sell only soda
with a door painted three colours, none of them on purpose
where the saloon’s back window was the only lamp

res-backhouse.proper: {V}’s house at Number Eleven and a Half, {street}, the half being the house in back
epithets: the half of an address the mailman had to be told about
which the city had never been told about at all
where the only light came from the big house’s kitchen

res-backhouse.proper: {V}’s house on the back lot off {street}, next to the pigeon coops
epithets: next door to a man who kept pigeons and loved them out loud
where the cooing started before anybody else was up
with a yard that was mostly feathers

rooftop.proper: the roof over the Dover apartments on {street}
epithets: with two water tanks squatting at the ends like a pair of old aunts
where the tar went soft in July and stayed sticky till October
with a view of every other roof and none of the sky

rooftop.proper: the roof over the Belvedere on {avenue}, with the pigeon loft
epithets: where the pigeons held the lease and everybody else was a guest
with a loft of pigeons who took an interest in visitors
that murmured like a crowd even when nobody was on it

rooftop.proper: the roof over the tenement at {street} and {avenue}, which the block called Tar Beach
epithets: where the block went to sleep on hot nights and to sunbathe on hot days
with a clothesline strung between every two things that stood still
sticky underfoot from May to September

rooftop.proper: the roof over the Grayson building on {street}, under the big sign for Dr. Hopewell’s Liver Pills
epithets: under a sign promising a new liver to the whole avenue
in the shadow of a painted doctor with a very trustworthy moustache
where the sign’s bulbs buzzed like a summer porch

rooftop.proper: the roof over Engel’s bakery on {avenue}
epithets: warm underfoot from the ovens even in January
that smelled of bread at every hour but the useful ones
where the chimney breathed out cinnamon

rooftop.proper: the roof of the Ardmore apartments on {street}, with the garden nobody watered
epithets: with tomato plants in tin cans, most of them long past saving
where somebody had once put out deck chairs and then lost interest
with a trellis that had given up and lain down

rooftop.proper: {V}’s corner of the roof over the building on {street}, with the tar-paper shed
epithets: with a tar-paper shed {V} called the summer house
where {V} had set out two kitchen chairs and called it a terrace
which the rest of the building visited by invitation only

back-alley.proper: the alley behind Rubin’s delicatessen off {street}
epithets: that smelled of pickle brine and ash cans in equal parts
where the crates of empty jars stood taller than a man
lit by one bulb over Rubin’s back door

back-alley.proper: the alley behind Koenig’s delicatessen on {avenue}, between the smokehouse and the stable
epithets: where the smokehouse had been curing the bricks for thirty years
that smelled of hickory smoke and horse
with a drain in the middle that everything ran toward, eventually

back-alley.proper: the alley behind Glick’s delicatessen off {street}, which the block called Pickle Alley
epithets: where the pickle barrels waited to be taken in and never quite were
slick with brine in patches
that a man could find in the dark by nose alone

back-alley.proper: the alley behind the Bon Ton Delicatessen off {avenue}
epithets: behind a delicatessen whose name promised more than its sandwiches
where the Bon Ton’s cook sat on a crate to smoke and argue with nobody
with a back door painted green in 1910 and not since

back-alley.proper: the gap behind Pappas’s delicatessen on {street}, where the fire escapes met
epithets: where six fire escapes met overhead in a tangle like dropped knitting
wide enough for a delivery cart and no wider
where the washing hung overhead like the flags of a small, poor country

back-alley.proper: the alley behind DiNapoli’s delicatessen off {street}, under the hanging provolone
epithets: under a back window where the provolone hung to cure like fat church lamps
that smelled of olive oil and garlic and whatever the ash cans added
where a bicycle had been chained to a drainpipe since before the war
where {V} stacked the empty crates a little higher every week
lit by the bulb over {V}’s back door
which {V} swept every morning and nobody else ever did

office-over-tailor.proper: the office over Abruzzo’s tailor shop on {street}
epithets: that smelled of steam and hot wool from the pressing irons below
over a window full of suits on headless dummies
with a frosted-glass door that had worn three different names in gold

office-over-tailor.proper: the office over Fishbein the tailor on {avenue}, under the gold-leaf sign
epithets: over a tailor who hemmed trousers while you waited and judged you while he did it
where the steam from the pressing machine came up through the floor
under a gold-leaf sign that read ALTERATIONS and meant it

office-over-tailor.proper: the office over the Imperial Tailoring Company on {street}
epithets: over a company that was one tailor and his brother-in-law
where a dress dummy stood on the landing like a headless hostess
with a door that stuck until you said please

office-over-tailor.proper: the office over Szabo’s tailor shop on {street}, up the stair with the brass rail
epithets: up a stair with a brass rail polished by nervous hands
over a tailor who talked to his suits in Hungarian
that smelled of tailor’s chalk and pressed wool

office-over-tailor.proper: the office over Moe’s Suits Pressed While You Wait on {street}
epithets: over a sign promising suits pressed while you wait, and people did wait
where the iron below hissed every few minutes like it had heard something shocking
with a window that looked straight into a laundry across the street

office-over-tailor.proper: the office over Donatelli & Son, Tailors, on {avenue}
epithets: over a shop where the son was sixty and still called the boy
with bolts of cloth in the window going pale in the sun
up a stair so narrow you had to let the other fellow finish first

office-over-tailor.proper: {V}’s office over the tailor’s shop on {street}
epithets: with {V}’s name lettered in gold on the frosted glass
where {V} kept the blinds half down in all weathers
that smelled of pressing steam from the tailor’s downstairs

pier-shed.proper: Pier 46, under the shed at the foot of {street}
epithets: where the river slapped the pilings like it had a grudge
under a tin roof that boomed in any wind
that smelled of tar, rope and oranges off the fruit boats

pier-shed.proper: the banana shed on Pier 14 at the foot of {street}
epithets: where the air was thick with green bananas going yellow
with a story about a tarantula that every dockworker told and nobody had seen
where the crates were stacked three high and labelled in Spanish

pier-shed.proper: the coal shed on the railroad pier off {street}
epithets: where everything, including the air, was a little bit black
with a coal chute that roared like a waterfall when it ran
where a white shirt lasted about a minute

pier-shed.proper: the fish pier at the foot of {street}, under the long shed
epithets: that smelled of Friday every day of the week
where the gulls outnumbered the men and outshouted them
with planks that were never quite dry and never quite clean

pier-shed.proper: the Mulvaney Towing shed on the pier at the foot of {street}
epithets: where the tugboats sat nose to the pilings like cab horses waiting for a fare
with MULVANEY TOWING painted on the roof for the benefit of the gulls
that shook whenever a tug bumped in

pier-shed.proper: the freight shed on Pier 61 off {street}
epithets: with a freight door as big as a church front
where the hand trucks stood in rows like a parked army
that echoed like the inside of a drum whenever anybody walked on it

pier-shed.proper: the sugar shed on Pier 22 off {street}
epithets: where the planks were sticky and the flies were in heaven
that smelled like the inside of a candy jar left in the sun
with burst sacks swept into sweet grey drifts in the corners

laundry-yard.proper: the drying yard behind Quong’s laundry on {street}
epithets: strung with more clotheslines than a ship has ropes
where the steam hung in the air long after the irons were cold
damp underfoot in every season

laundry-yard.proper: the drying yard behind the Pioneer Steam Laundry on {avenue}
epithets: behind a laundry that boiled the whole block’s collars
where the lines creaked in the wind like a ship’s rigging
that smelled of lye soap strong enough to clean a conscience

laundry-yard.proper: the yard behind Mrs. O’Dwyer’s hand laundry on {street}
epithets: where Mrs. O’Dwyer’s sheets were the whitest in the ward, and she would tell you so
with a tin tub the size of a rowboat by the back door
where a holy picture was nailed up to keep an eye on the wash

laundry-yard.proper: the yard behind the Monarch Wet Wash on {avenue}
epithets: behind a laundry that sent your wash home wet and your socks home as strangers
where the lines sagged under sheets as heavy as sails
that dripped from every line like a cave

laundry-yard.proper: the drying yard behind Hirsch’s French Hand Laundry on {street}
epithets: behind a French laundry about as French as the fire hydrant
where the lace curtains of the whole neighbourhood dried side by side
that smelled of starch and scorched cotton

laundry-yard.proper: the drying yard behind Hop Kee’s laundry on {street}, which the block called the Kite Yard
epithets: where the sheets went up like kites in a good wind
walled in on three sides by the backs of buildings
where you learned to duck without being told

laundry-yard.proper: the drying yard behind {V}’s laundry on {street}
epithets: strung with {V}’s own lines, knotted {V}’s own way
which {V} swept and watered down like a front parlour
with {V}’s washtubs stacked by the back door

walkup-flat.proper: the third-floor front in the walk-up on {avenue}, over Kostas’s shoeshine stand
epithets: over a shoeshine stand that smelled of polish and gossip
with three front windows on the avenue and a draught for each
where the banister came loose in two places and you learned which

walkup-flat.proper: the third floor of the Rosalind, a walk-up on {street}
local: the third floor at the Rosalind
epithets: whose name was carved over the door with more confidence than the building deserved
where every step had its own complaint
with a skylight over the stair so grey it counted as a wall

walkup-flat.proper: the third-floor flat over Vasquez’s cigar store on {avenue}
epithets: that smelled of cigar leaf all the way up the stairs
over a store where men rolled cigars in the window
with a wooden figure at the street door that the block said good evening to

walkup-flat.proper: the third floor of the walk-up at {street} and {avenue} with the busted lamp out front
local: the building with the busted lamp
epithets: with a busted lamp out front the city had been fixing since the Taft administration
where the halls were dark enough to count your steps
up three flights that each felt longer than the last

walkup-flat.proper: the third-floor rear in the Dunmore walk-up on {street}
epithets: that looked out on a yard full of other people’s washing
where the hall smelled of six dinners at once
with walls thin enough to follow a neighbour’s argument without leaning in

walkup-flat.proper: the third-floor flat over the Paradise Candy Store on {avenue}
epithets: over a candy store the children called Paradise without a trace of irony
where the stairs were sticky from generations of lollipops
that smelled of burnt sugar up to the landing

walkup-flat.proper: the third-floor flat in the wedge-shaped walk-up at {street} and {avenue}
epithets: narrow at one end like a slice of pie
where the corner room was too thin for a bed and too wide for a closet
with windows on three sides and heat on none

hallam-vestibule.proper: the vestibule of the Hallam apartments on {street}
epithets: all marble and brass and the feeling you should wipe your feet twice
with brass mailboxes polished to the point of vanity
where the glass doors locked themselves and took a certain pleasure in it

hallam-vestibule.proper: the vestibule of the Chatsworth on {avenue}
epithets: a building that wanted you to know it had an elevator
with a doormat monogrammed like a bath towel
where the potted palms were real and seemed surprised about it

hallam-vestibule.proper: the vestibule of the Sherwood Arms on {street}, with the mural of Robin Hood
epithets: under a painted Robin Hood who had robbed nobody in thirty years
with a marble floor that rang under every heel
where the long mirror had watched a great many hats adjusted

hallam-vestibule.proper: the vestibule of the Beaumont on {avenue}, the apartment house with the green awning
epithets: under a green awning that ran all the way to the curb in case of royalty
where the tenants’ names were engraved, not typed
with a night buzzer loud enough to wake the fourth floor

hallam-vestibule.proper: the vestibule of the Kenilworth on {street}
epithets: with marble so white it looked embarrassed by the street
that smelled of floor polish and money
with a bench nobody sat on for longer than it took to be looked at

hallam-vestibule.proper: the vestibule of Van Dam Court on {street}
epithets: which was not a court and had never met a Van Dam
with its name cut in stone over the door as if it meant to last forever
where even the radiator cover was marble, to be safe

hallam-vestibule.proper: the vestibule of the Montague on {avenue}, the building with the stone gargoyles
epithets: under four stone gargoyles who had seen worse
where a crack in the marble floor was what the super called character
with mailboxes for forty tenants and names on thirty

rooming-house-room.proper: the back room at Mrs. {W}’s rooming house on {street}
epithets: where the house rules were typed and pinned to every door
with a runner on the stairs worn through to the boards in a path
where grace before supper was not optional

rooming-house-room.proper: the back room at the Laurel House, Mrs. {W}’s rooming house on {street}
epithets: with a laurel in a tub by the door that had been failing since the Armistice
where the back room sat over the kitchen and got every smell first
where the boarders ate in shifts and argued in all of them

rooming-house-room.proper: the back room at Mrs. {W}’s theatrical rooming house on {avenue}
epithets: where every boarder had once been almost famous
with playbills pasted up the stairs like wallpaper
where somebody was always rehearsing a farewell speech behind a door

rooming-house-room.proper: the back room at the Hotel Kilkenny, which was Mrs. {W}’s rooming house with ideas, on {street}
epithets: a rooming house that had painted HOTEL on its window and hoped
where the sheets were changed on Saturdays whether they needed it or not
with a hall table where the mail lay for days and got read by everybody

rooming-house-room.proper: the back room at Mrs. {W}’s on {street}, the house with the brass plate that said ROOMS
epithets: with a brass plate on the door that said ROOMS and nothing else
where the lace curtains twitched whenever anybody came up the stoop
with a hall so narrow the boarders had worked out a rule for passing

rooming-house-room.proper: the back room at Mrs. {W}’s boarding house for Respectable Gentlemen on {avenue}
epithets: for respectable gentlemen, which ruled out most of the boarders
where the stairs had been waxed into a hazard
that smelled of boiled beef and carpet soap
the cheapest room in the house, and {V} knew it
where {V} kept everything worth keeping under the bed
with {V}’s name on a card tacked to the door
where the sawdust on the floor got changed at Easter
with a painted name over the door and not one other word
where a stranger got served and stared at, in that order
which had not grilled anything since 1920
where the free lunch was a hard-boiled egg and a warning
under a tin ceiling the colour of old tea

dolans-bar.proper: the Shamrock Café on {avenue}, a bar that had called itself a café since the law changed
epithets: a bar that had been a café ever since the law changed, and fooled nobody
with a shamrock in the window faded to the colour of lettuce
where the corned beef came with the glass whether you asked or not

dolans-bar.proper: Kowalczyk’s on {street}, the bar with the moose head
epithets: under a moose head the regulars toasted by name
where nobody could spell the owner’s name and everybody could say it
that smelled of kielbasa and spilled beer

dolans-bar.proper: the Hofbrau on {avenue}, the German bar with the long tables
epithets: with long wooden tables built for arguing
where the pretzels were free and the mustard was hot enough to clear a head cold
under a painted Bavarian mountain on the back wall

dolans-bar.proper: the Silver Dollar on {street}, the bar with silver dollars set in the floor
epithets: with silver dollars set in the floor under the rail, and men who had tried to pry them up
where the tiles were cracked in the shape of old fights
with a swinging door that only swung one way

dolans-bar.proper: McGlade’s on {avenue}, the bar the firemen from the engine house used
epithets: where the firemen from the engine house drank and told the same fire twice
with a brass fire nozzle over the door for luck
which emptied in one minute flat whenever the engine house turned out
with {V}’s name painted over the door and nothing else
where {V} kept the good bottles out of sight and the bad ones out of reach
which {V} opened every morning and closed whenever

speakeasy.proper: the speakeasy under Madame Rochelle’s hat shop on {street}
epithets: six steps down under a window full of hats nobody bought
where the knock on the door was a formality and everybody knew it
behind a door with a slot that opened for anybody who looked thirsty

speakeasy.proper: the Brim, the speakeasy under Greenbaum’s hat shop on {avenue}
epithets: named for the hats upstairs and full to the brim most nights
with a ceiling so low the tall men drank bowing
where the gin came in teacups, in case anyone asked

speakeasy.proper: the cellar under the Parisian Hat Shoppe on {street}, which the whole block called the Parish
epithets: called the Parish because its regulars went there more faithfully than to church
under a hat shop that spelled shop with two p’s and an e
where the password changed every week and nobody bothered to learn it

speakeasy.proper: the speakeasy under Mrs. Fogarty’s hat shop on {avenue}, down the old coal-chute stairs
epithets: down stairs that had been a coal chute and still felt like one
where the bar was three doors laid across barrels
where every hat ended up on a peg its owner hadn’t chosen

speakeasy.proper: the Velvet Room, under the hat shop at {street} and {avenue}
epithets: with red velvet on the walls that had been a theatre curtain in a better life
where the velvet soaked up the smoke and never gave it back
that made you whisper even when you didn’t mean to

speakeasy.proper: the speakeasy under Bellini Brothers Hats on {street}
epithets: under a hat shop that sold one hat a week and never seemed to mind
where the wine came in coffee cups and the coffee didn’t come at all
with a trapdoor behind the bar that everybody pretended not to see

speakeasy.proper: the Owl’s Nest, the speakeasy under the hat shop on {avenue}
epithets: open all night, as the name promised
with a painted owl on the door slot, winking
where the regulars were pale from never seeing daylight

hotel-lobby.proper: the lobby of the Wyckoff on {avenue}
epithets: with a red carpet worn thin by a million trips to the elevator
where the spittoons were polished brighter than the guests
with a revolving door that stuck if you pushed it like you meant it

hotel-lobby.proper: the lobby of the Hotel Continental on {street}
epithets: which had seen better decades and kept the furniture from all of them
under a chandelier that had lost a third of its crystals and none of its pride
where the lobby chairs held the shape of the last man who sat in them

hotel-lobby.proper: the lobby of the Van Cortlandt House on {avenue}
epithets: with an oil painting of a Van Cortlandt nobody could name over the desk
where the potted palms had been there longer than the staff
that smelled of cigar smoke and furniture polish

hotel-lobby.proper: the lobby of the Hotel Alcazar on {street}, done up Spanish
epithets: done up Spanish, with tiles, arches and a fountain that hadn’t run since the war
where every arch had a potted palm and every palm had a cigar butt in it
which tried hard to be Seville and mostly got as far as Hoboken

hotel-lobby.proper: the lobby of the Hotel Metropole on {avenue}, the one with the gilded elevator
epithets: with a gilded elevator cage like a birdcage for a very rich bird
with more mirrors than a barber shop
where the rooms were by the night and the gossip was free

hotel-lobby.proper: the lobby of the Hotel Albemarle on {street}, all dark wood and deep chairs
epithets: with chairs deep enough to lose a man in
where the carpet swallowed footsteps whole
with a writing desk whose hotel stationery walked off steadily

hotel-lobby.proper: the lobby of the Hotel Royal Palms on {avenue}
epithets: which had one palm, in a tub, and nothing royal about it
where the brass had been polished so often it had gone thin
with a sign by the elevator forbidding cooking in the rooms, and a smell that said somebody did

corner-newsstand.proper: the newsstand on the corner of {street} and {avenue}
epithets: under a corrugated roof that drummed in any weather
with a bulb hung over the headlines for anybody reading after dark
which had held the corner since before the buildings went up

corner-newsstand.proper: the newsstand under the El stairs at {street} and {avenue}
epithets: in the shadow of the El stairs all day and all night
where the magazines hung on clothespins like washing
which sold chewing gum, cigarettes and opinions

corner-newsstand.proper: the newsstand outside Pincus’s cigar store at {street} and {avenue}
epithets: leaning on Pincus’s cigar store like a tired friend
where the pages with the horse races sold out before anything else
with a tin roof and a canvas flap for the wind

corner-newsstand.proper: the green newsstand at the foot of the church steps on {street}
epithets: painted the same green as the church door, which was either piety or a bargain on paint
where the Sunday funnies were sold straight after Mass
with a wooden box to stand on for anybody short enough to need it

corner-newsstand.proper: the newsstand at {street} and {avenue} with the magazines in six languages
epithets: selling magazines in six languages and gossip in all of them
where the whole world’s headlines hung on clothespins, in no particular order
with a pile of foreign magazines held down by a brick

corner-newsstand.proper: the newsstand against the granite wall of the post office on {avenue}
local: the stand by the post office
epithets: against a granite wall that made the stand look like it had wandered into church
the only thing on the corner open after the post office shut
with a tin roof painted to look like shingles, and fooling nobody
where {V} had stood through twenty winters and complained about each one
with a padlocked cupboard underneath that {V} guarded like a bank vault
hung with {V}’s magazines on clothespins
with a wall of little glass doors, each hiding a slice of pie and a hope
where the coffee came out of a brass dolphin’s mouth
which never closed and never looked like it wanted to

automat.proper: the big Automat on {avenue} with the marble counters
epithets: with marble counters and brass fittings, like a bank that sold beans
where a nickel bought a cup of coffee and an hour of sitting
lit like an operating room at every hour

automat.proper: the little Automat on {street} next to the telegraph office
epithets: half the size of the big ones and twice as lonely at night
where the pie doors stuck and you had to know the trick
that smelled of coffee and floor soap round the clock

automat.proper: the Automat at {street} and {avenue}, the one the chorus girls used
epithets: where the chorus girls ate baked beans in full make-up between shows
with mirrors on every wall, so nobody ever ate alone
where the cashier could turn a dollar into twenty nickels without looking

automat.proper: the Automat on {avenue} across from the armory
epithets: across from the armory, so half the customers had haircuts to match
where the macaroni and cheese had a following
with a brass nickel slot under every little door

automat.proper: the Automat at {street} and {avenue} with the stained-glass front
epithets: with a two-storey stained-glass window, as if a cathedral had gone into the lunch business
where the light came through the glass in colours and landed on the creamed spinach
which took itself very seriously for a place that sold pie through a slot

automat.proper: the Automat on {street} that everybody called the Nickel Palace
epithets: a palace of nickels, where every nickel got counted twice
where lonely people came to sit near other lonely people
with rows of little lit windows like an Advent calendar
with a marquee that had lost three letters and gained a pigeon
where the red carpet had gone pink down the middle
that smelled of hot peanuts and wet coats

movie-house.proper: the Gem Theatre on {street}, a picture house with four hundred seats
epithets: four hundred seats and two good ones
where you could hear the projector clatter like a sewing machine from the lobby
with posters in glass cases for pictures that had closed a month ago

movie-house.proper: the Alhambra picture palace on {avenue}, all arches and plaster stars
epithets: with a ceiling painted like a night sky over somewhere warmer
all Moorish arches and plaster camels
where the ushers dressed like doormen from a better hotel

movie-house.proper: the Star Theatre on {street}, the picture house the block called the Scratch House
epithets: called the Scratch House on account of what lived in the seats
where a dime bought two pictures and a newsreel
with a balcony that swayed when the audience laughed

movie-house.proper: the Majestic on {avenue}, the big picture house with the balcony
epithets: with a balcony so high the screen looked like a postage stamp
where the ushers carried flashlights like altar boys with candles
with a lobby of gilt mirrors that made any crowd look twice as big
which called itself a photoplay house, having been built before anybody settled on a word
where the cowboy pictures ran on Saturdays and the romances the rest of the week
that smelled of sweeping compound and cigar
where half the customers came to sleep somewhere warm for a dime
with a painted moon over the screen that somebody had given a moustache
whose ticket booth was shaped like a little castle
with a floor waxed so slick the timid danced by holding on
where the band played louder than it played well
that smelled of floor wax and hair oil

dance-hall.proper: the Rosebud Ballroom on {street}, ten cents a dance
epithets: ten cents a dance and no refunds
where the dancing partners wore their tickets on a string like pearls
with paper roses on every pillar, going brown at the edges

dance-hall.proper: the Starlight Roof, the dance hall over the furniture store on {avenue}
epithets: over a furniture store, so every foxtrot shook the sofas downstairs
under a ceiling of little electric stars, some of them working
where the saxophone could be heard three blocks off
an academy where nobody had learned a step since it opened
with a painted sign promising the tango in six easy lessons
where the mirrors on the walls were kind to nobody

dance-hall.proper: the Golden Slipper on {avenue}, the dance hall with the mirrored ball
epithets: under a ball of little mirrors that threw spots of light across everybody like confetti
with a gold slipper the size of a bathtub over the door
where the foxtrot went on longer than the dancers did

dance-hall.proper: the Hibernian Hall on {street}, where the Irish danced on Saturdays
epithets: where the Saturday reels shook the dust off the rafters
with a portrait of a stern bishop keeping an eye on the dancing
that smelled of beer served in teapots and wet wool
which had given up the tango years ago and kept the name for luck
where the band sat behind a row of potted ferns like men in hiding
with a sprung floor that bounced under a crowd

drugstore.proper: Kaplan’s drugstore with the soda fountain, on {avenue}
epithets: with a soda fountain that made the best egg cream on the avenue
where the bottles behind the counter were labelled in a hand that hadn’t changed in thirty years
that smelled of vanilla syrup and iodine

drugstore.proper: Brodsky’s drugstore on {street}, the one with the marble soda fountain
epithets: with a marble soda fountain as long as a streetcar
where the children spun the fountain seats round and round
which sold a cough syrup the block drank for reasons unrelated to coughing
under a gilded crown over the door that was missing two points
where the soda jerk could build a sundae like a cathedral
which sold corn plasters, face cream and nerve tonic off the same counter

drugstore.proper: Rossi’s drugstore on {avenue}, where the grandmothers bought camphor
epithets: where the grandmothers of the block bought camphor by the pound
with a soda fountain the owner’s son ran like a stage show
that smelled of camphor, almond and cigars

drugstore.proper: the Victory Drug Company on {street}, with the big mortar and pestle over the door
epithets: under a wooden mortar and pestle the size of a beer keg
whose window promised cures for coughs, bad feet and the blues
with a scale by the door that told you your weight and your fortune for a penny

drugstore.proper: Whitlock’s drugstore on {avenue}, the one with the soda fountain everybody stopped at
epithets: where the whole avenue stopped for a soda on the way home
with a sign in the window promising prescriptions filled carefully, and a second sign promising it again
that smelled of ginger ale and floor oil
where {V} had filled prescriptions for twenty years without once smiling
with {V}’s diploma framed by the register where the customers could check it
where {V} kept the back room locked and the front room spotless

cab-stand.proper: the cab stand outside the Hippodrome
epithets: outside a theatre so big they once made an elephant vanish on its stage
where the cabbies kept their engines warm and their opinions warmer
with a line painted on the curb that the cabs obeyed and the pigeons didn’t

cab-stand.proper: the cab stand outside the Gaiety Theatre on {street}
epithets: outside a burlesque house that had painted over the word burlesque
where the cabbies argued about baseball in three languages
under a marquee with more bulbs out than in

cab-stand.proper: the cab stand outside the Lyric on {avenue}, by the fire hydrant
epithets: by a fire hydrant every cabbie swore he wasn’t parked at
outside a theatre that had played the same operetta for two years
where the cabs lined up yellow and black like a row of wasps

cab-stand.proper: the cab stand outside the Yiddish theatre on Second Avenue
local: the stand by the Yiddish theatre
epithets: outside a theatre where every play ended in tears and then a wedding
where the cabbies knew the plots better than the actors did
under a marquee in letters half the cabbies couldn’t read and all of them could quote

cab-stand.proper: the cab stand outside the Lafayette Theatre on Seventh Avenue
epithets: beside the tree the performers touched for luck on their way to auditions
where the cabbies had heard every good band on the avenue through the walls
under a marquee that stayed lit longer than the rest of the avenue

cab-stand.proper: the cab stand outside the Empire Music Hall on {avenue}
epithets: outside a music hall whose poster lady had faded through twelve summers
where the cabbies ate their sandwiches on the running boards
where one raised hand could bring three cabs and a fight

cab-stand.proper: the cab stand outside the Casino Theatre on {street}
epithets: outside a theatre called the Casino that had never taken a bet in its life
where the cabbies played checkers on an upturned crate
with a streetlamp that leaned toward the stand like it wanted a ride

tenement-stairwell.proper: the stairwell of the tenement on {street}
epithets: where every tread was worn to a dip in the middle
that smelled of six floors of dinners at once
lit by a bare bulb on every other landing, to save money

tenement-stairwell.proper: the stairwell of the Bella Vista tenement on {street}
epithets: named for a beautiful view it did not have
where a window on each landing looked out, closely, at the building next door
with a banister polished by children sliding down it

tenement-stairwell.proper: the stairwell of the six-storey tenement at {street} and {avenue} with the saint in the front hall
epithets: with a plaster saint in a niche in the front hall and a candle always lit at his feet
where the neighbours left their doors open for the air and their business open with them
that carried six floors of arguments in four languages
where six floors shared one stair and one opinion of the landlord
with pressed-tin walls painted the colour of pea soup
which nobody had swept since the Armistice

tenement-stairwell.proper: the stairwell of the Garibaldi Flats on {street}
epithets: named for a hero on horseback who would never have fit up the stairs
where the landings were stacked with baby carriages and bicycles
that smelled of garlic on one floor and cabbage on the next

tenement-stairwell.proper: the back stairwell of the tenement over Feld’s shoe store on {street}
epithets: over a shoe store whose smell of leather reached the second landing
with a skylight at the top that let in more pigeons than light
where every step groaned in a different key

tenement-stairwell.proper: the landing outside {V}’s door in the tenement on {street}
epithets: outside {V}’s door, which had three locks and a holy picture
where {V} kept a kitchen chair for the cool of the evening
which {V} scrubbed on Saturdays, whether it was {V}’s turn or not
where the smoke hung over the tables like a second ceiling
where the green felt had seen better shots and worse men
that smelled of chalk, cigars and wet wool

pool-hall.proper: the Cue Club, down the stairs at {street} and {avenue}
epithets: which called itself a club so it could keep out whoever it liked
where the good table was at the back and so were the good players
with a spittoon by every table and a sign asking you to use it

pool-hall.proper: Karras’s billiard parlour on {street}, eight tables and a lunch counter
epithets: eight tables and a lunch counter, and the lunch counter was the bigger hazard
where the balls clicked like a telegraph office
with a sign over the door that said GENTLEMEN ONLY and customers who had not read it

pool-hall.proper: the Corner Pocket on {avenue}, under the barber college
epithets: under a barber college where the students practised on anybody brave enough
where the lamps hung so low the tall players got a tan
with a floor you didn’t look at too closely

pool-hall.proper: Sokol’s pool hall on {street}, the long room with the tin ceiling
epithets: a room so long the far tables were a rumour
under a pressed-tin ceiling brown with fifty years of smoke
where the score was kept on wooden beads strung overhead like an abacus
an academy with no diploma and plenty of homework
where the cues were chained to the wall after a certain incident
where the clack of the balls carried up to the street

pool-hall.proper: Mahoney’s billiard hall on {street}, over the harness maker’s
epithets: over a harness maker’s, so the whole place smelled faintly of saddle
where the chalk dust got into everything including the coffee
with a window so dirty the daylight had to knock

pawnshop.proper: the back room of Zelinsky’s pawnshop on {street}
epithets: behind a curtain that never quite closed
under three gold balls that had lost most of their gold
where a hundred things nobody had come back for sat waiting anyway

pawnshop.proper: the back room of Uncle Ike’s Loan Office on {avenue}
epithets: where the block had pawned its Sunday suits every Monday for thirty years
behind a window full of trumpets, banjos and one stuffed alligator
where the back room smelled of mothballs and other people’s luck

pawnshop.proper: the back room of Moskowitz’s pawnshop on {street}
epithets: behind a grille that came down with a noise like a dropped drawer of cutlery
where the shelves went up to the ceiling and the ladder only halfway
with a desk buried under things that hadn’t been decided about yet

pawnshop.proper: the back room of the Golden Rule Loan Company on {avenue}
epithets: which was one pawnbroker and his mother, and the mother did the pricing
under a sign reading WE BUY GOLD that had worn down to WE BUY OLD
where the back room was a museum of bad luck

pawnshop.proper: the back room of Fiorello’s pawnshop on {street}, behind the accordions
epithets: behind a wall of pawned accordions that wheezed whenever the door slammed
where nobody had come back for the violin in twelve years
that smelled of brass polish and old leather

pawnshop.proper: the back room of the Friendly Loan Office on {avenue}
epithets: friendly about everything but the interest
with a barred window on a brick wall close enough to lick
where the pawned wedding dresses hung in a row like brides at the wrong church

pawnshop.proper: the back room of {V}’s pawnshop on {street}
epithets: where {V} kept what wasn’t for sale
behind {V}’s counter and {V}’s curtain
where {V} did the accounts under a single bulb

chop-suey.proper: the chop suey place over the laundry on {street}
epithets: up a stair with a paper lantern at the bottom
where the tea came in a pot big enough to bathe in
with a calendar on the wall two months behind and in no hurry

chop-suey.proper: the Canton Garden, the chop suey place over the Wah Lee laundry on {avenue}
epithets: which had no garden but one very determined paper plum tree
where the egg foo young came out the size of a hubcap
open later than anything else on the avenue and proud of it

chop-suey.proper: the Oriental Chop Suey over Lee’s hand laundry on {street}
epithets: up a stair lit by a red sign that said CHOP SUEY and nothing else
where the tables were so close you ate your neighbour’s conversation with your noodles
with a jade-green door at the top of the stair

chop-suey.proper: the Golden Dragon chop suey house over the laundry at {street} and {avenue}
epithets: under a painted dragon that had lost its tail to the weather
where the chow mein was a dime and the conversation was free
that smelled of hot oil and ginger all the way down to the street

chop-suey.proper: Mock’s chop suey place over the laundry on {street}
epithets: open till daylight and a little past
where the cook and the waiter argued through a hatch all night
with booths along one wall and a curtain for each

chop-suey.proper: the Far East Tea Garden over the laundry on {avenue}
epithets: where the tea came in teapots and sometimes wasn’t tea
with a string of paper lanterns across the ceiling, half of them lit
that smelled of jasmine and frying onions

chop-suey.proper: {V}’s chop suey place over the laundry on {street}
epithets: where {V} kept the cash register close and the recipes closer
with {V}’s name on the lantern at the foot of the stair
where {V} knew every customer’s order before the coat was off

boarding-parlor.proper: the parlour of Mrs. {W}’s boarding house on {street}
epithets: with a horsehair sofa nobody sat on twice
where lace covers were pinned to every chair back like napkins at a banquet
that smelled of lavender polish and boiled supper

boarding-parlor.proper: the front parlour of the Magnolia House, Mrs. {W}’s boarding house on {avenue}
epithets: with wax magnolias under a glass dome, the only flowers that ever lasted a winter there
kept for callers who never called
where a fern in a brass tub was the oldest boarder in the house

boarding-parlor.proper: the parlour of Mrs. {W}’s house for business girls on {street}
epithets: where gentleman callers were received with the door wide open
with the house rules on the wall, numbered, all the way to twenty-two
that smelled of face cream and hot curling irons

boarding-parlor.proper: the parlour of the Harwood, Mrs. {W}’s boarding house on {avenue}
epithets: which had been a sea captain’s house and still had his brass telescope in the window
where the ship in a bottle on the mantel was the only thing in the house that had travelled
with wallpaper of ships sailing nowhere in rows

boarding-parlor.proper: the parlour of the Sailors’ Rest, Mrs. {W}’s boarding house on {street}
epithets: where the sailors were asked to rest quietly and mostly didn’t
with a painted lifebuoy over the mantel
that smelled of pipe tobacco and salt-stiff wool

boarding-parlor.proper: the parlour of Mrs. {W}’s on {street}, the house with the stained-glass fanlight
epithets: under a stained-glass fanlight that threw coloured diamonds on the hall floor
where the good china lived behind glass and never came out
with a bowl of wax fruit nobody had been fooled by since 1900

boarding-parlor.proper: the parlour of the Dunleavy House on {avenue}, which Mrs. {W} ran like a convent
epithets: run like a convent, with fewer candles and more rules
where the chairs stood in a circle for conversations nobody wanted
where you sat up straight without being told
with a striped pole out front that turned whether anybody was coming or not
where three chairs faced a mirror and the mirror faced back
where the talk was baseball until somebody said a name
which called itself tonsorial and meant barber
with a shoeshine boy asleep on the waiting bench
where the hot towels came out of a steamer like dumplings

barber-shop.proper: Schmitt’s barber shop on {avenue}, with the hair tonic in the window
epithets: with a pyramid of hair tonic in the window promising a full head by Easter
where old Schmitt had been cutting the same heads since they had hair on them
that smelled of talc and lilac water

barber-shop.proper: the Eureka barber shop on {street}, under the pole with the missing stripe
epithets: under a barber pole missing one stripe, like a candy cane somebody had bitten
where the waiting bench was the neighbourhood’s parliament
with a leather strop hanging by every chair like a tongue

barber-shop.proper: Mitchell’s barber shop on {avenue}, the one with the shoeshine stand
epithets: where the whole avenue came to be shaved and to settle arguments
with a shoeshine stand by the door raised up like a throne
where the talk ran on long after the haircuts stopped

barber-shop.proper: Figaro’s, the barber shop on {street} named for the opera
epithets: named for an opera barber and run by a man who had never seen an opera
with a gramophone that played the same three records
where a shave came with a hot towel and a lecture on the tariff
with {V}’s own chair at the front by the window
where {V} kept the good razors locked in a drawer
with {V}’s name in gold on the glass
that smelled of gasoline clear out to the sidewalk
with oil stains on the floor in the shape of every car that had ever parked there
where the rolling door groaned like a man getting out of bed

hotel-garage.proper: the Keystone Garage on {street}, where the hotels sent their guests’ cars
epithets: where the hotels sent their guests’ cars to be kept out of sight and out of trouble
with a row of limousines under canvas like horses in blankets
where somebody’s feet were sticking out from under a car most hours of the day

hotel-garage.proper: the garage on {avenue} that used to be the Metropolitan livery stable
epithets: which had been a stable and still had the hay hooks in the ceiling
where the ramp to the second floor had been built for horses
that smelled of motor oil with a little horse underneath

hotel-garage.proper: the Speedwell Garage on {street}, the one with the gasoline pump out front
epithets: with a gasoline pump out front shaped like a lighthouse
where the tires were stacked like a giant’s checkers
that echoed like a railway station whenever a door slammed

hotel-garage.proper: Gallagher’s Garage and Taxi Repair on {avenue}
epithets: where the cabs came in coughing and went out swearing
with a calendar of pretty girls holding spark plugs
that smelled of burnt clutch and coffee

hotel-garage.proper: the Sterling Motor Garage on {street}, four floors of cars with an elevator for them
epithets: with a car elevator big enough for a Packard and slow enough to read a book on
four floors of cars sleeping under canvas
where the night lamps made the chrome look like a parade
where {V} knew every car by the sound of its engine
with {V}’s name painted over the door in letters a yard high
where {V} kept a cot in the office for the long nights

el-platform.proper: the uptown platform of the El at {street}
epithets: two storeys up on iron legs, with the whole street for a basement
where the wind came up through the planks from below
with a change booth at the top of the stairs like a sentry box nobody had posted anyone to

el-platform.proper: the Third Avenue El station at {street}
epithets: with a pot-bellied stove in the waiting room that was the warmest thing for blocks
where you could look straight into second-floor windows and usually wished you hadn’t
with iron stairs painted so many times the rivets had gone soft

el-platform.proper: the Sixth Avenue El station at {street}
epithets: over an avenue that lived its whole life in the shade of the tracks
with cinders drifting down onto the hats below
where the sunlight came through the ties in stripes, like a jail cell with ambitions

el-platform.proper: the Ninth Avenue El station at {street}
epithets: the oldest El in the city and determined to be the loudest
with a platform that swayed a little in the wind, for character
where the stair rail had been worn silver by a million gloves

el-platform.proper: the Second Avenue El station at {street}
epithets: looking down on pushcarts and up at washing
where the wooden platform had been patched with every kind of wood there was
with signs for corsets and cough drops all along the railing

el-platform.proper: the El platform over {street}, with the little station house
epithets: with a station house like a gingerbread cottage perched on iron stilts
where the pigeons roosted in the girders and dropped their opinions
that caught every wind off the river and kept it

el-platform.proper: the El station at {street} that the kids called the Birdcage
epithets: an iron birdcage for people, two storeys up
where the view of the neighbourhood was all rooftops and laundry
with a turnstile that took your nickel and made you think about it

el-platform.proper: the El platform at {street}, above the coal yard
epithets: above a coal yard, so everybody waiting went home a shade darker
where the stairs were iron and rang under every step
looking down into the coal heaps like a gull over a harbour

square-benches.proper: the benches by the dry fountain in Stuyvesant Square
epithets: where the pigeons held court
by a fountain that had been dry so long it had forgotten how
under elms old enough to remember Peter Stuyvesant’s wooden leg

square-benches.proper: the benches along the north walk of Tompkins Square
epithets: where the old men played chess in five languages and lost in all of them
under an elm that had heard more speeches than any politician
where the pushcart men came to rest their feet

square-benches.proper: the benches at the arch end of Washington Square
epithets: in sight of the big white arch
where the poets sat and the pigeons listened, which was more than the poets deserved
with chess tables that were never empty in daylight

square-benches.proper: the benches by the bandstand in Mount Morris Park
epithets: under the old iron fire tower on the hill
by a bandstand whose bands had gone home for the season
where the paths climbed like they had somewhere important to be

square-benches.proper: the benches outside the railings of Gramercy Park
epithets: outside the railings, since only the people with keys got to sit inside
looking in at a park locked up like a pantry
where the rich walked by without seeing the benches at all

square-benches.proper: the benches in Columbus Park, where Mulberry Bend used to be
epithets: where the worst block in the city had been torn down to make a lawn
where the old men rolled bocce balls in their Sunday hats
with Chinatown on one side and Little Italy on the other, and the benches in between

square-benches.proper: the benches by the dry fountain at the north end of the square off {street}
epithets: where the pigeons ran the place and let the people sit
by a stone fountain shut off for the season, or possibly the decade
with one lamp at the corner doing the work of four

square-benches.proper: the benches under the plane trees in the little triangle at {street} and {avenue}
epithets: in a park so small it was mostly its own railings
under two plane trees shedding bark like old wallpaper
where the traffic went round all three sides like a moat

square-benches.proper: the benches around the bronze general in the square on {street}
epithets: around a bronze general on a horse gone green with pigeons and weather
where the general’s sword pointed at the bakery across the street, which everybody agreed was fair
with a lamp at each corner and one of them working

square-benches.proper: the benches around the flagpole in the little park on {street}
epithets: around a flagpole with no flag, which the neighbourhood took personally
where the pigeons had worn a path of their own in the grass
with the park’s single lamp at the gate, doing its best

ferry-slip.proper: the ferry slip at the foot of {street}
epithets: where the street ran out of street and turned into river
with a waiting room whose benches had been polished by a million impatient trousers
that smelled of tar and river water and coal smoke off the boats

ferry-slip.proper: the Hoboken ferry slip at the foot of Christopher Street
epithets: where the boats left for Hoboken as if that were a treat
with a ferry house trimmed in green copper like a seaside pavilion
where the gulls rode the ferry for free and knew it

ferry-slip.proper: the Weehawken ferry at the foot of West Forty-Second Street
epithets: crossing to Weehawken, where the famous duel was, and nobody here let you forget it
with a row of lamps on the ferry house that doubled in the water
where the gangplank banged down like a judge’s hammer

ferry-slip.proper: the Long Island ferry slip at the foot of East Thirty-Fourth Street
epithets: where the ferry crossed to Long Island City and came back looking relieved
with a stove in the waiting room the regulars sat round like a campfire
that smelled of the gasworks up the shore

ferry-slip.proper: the Grand Street ferry slip, where the boats crossed to Williamsburg
epithets: where the Williamsburg boats came in low with pushcart men and their carts
with a waiting room that smelled of pickles and river
where the ramp rose and fell with the tide like a long sigh

ferry-slip.proper: the ferry slip at the foot of {street}, next to the fireboat station
epithets: next to a red fireboat that nobody had ever seen go anywhere
where the pilings wore green beards of weed
with a tide that came and went under the planks, talking to itself

ferry-slip.proper: the old ferry slip at the foot of {street}, under the big painted sign
epithets: under a sign that said FERRY in letters a yard high, in case of doubt
where the waiting room had one window and it faced the wrong way
with the river so close under the planks you could hear it thinking

ferry-slip.proper: the ferry slip at the foot of West 125th Street, where the boats crossed to Edgewater
epithets: where Harlem went to cross the river on a Sunday
with the Jersey cliffs standing up across the water like a wall
where the frankfurter man kept his cart going even in winter

ferry-slip.proper: the Twenty-Third Street ferry to Jersey City
epithets: where the Jersey commuters came off in a rush like a dropped drawer of forks
under a ferry house as big as a railway station and twice as draughty
that smelled of coal smoke and oysters
an iron-and-glass hut over a hole in the ground, like a greenhouse for commuters
where warm air came up the stairs smelling of pennies and wet cement
with a bulb over the top step and nothing much further down

subway-kiosk.proper: the subway kiosk at {street} and {avenue}, with the iron cupola
epithets: with an iron cupola on top like a bandstand that had lost its band
where the station name was set in blue and white tiles down the stairs, in case you forgot
with a draught up the stairs that could take a hat clean off

subway-kiosk.proper: the uptown subway entrance at {street} and {avenue}, between the two lamp posts
epithets: between two iron lamp posts with glass globes, like the gate of a very small palace
where the stairs went down as steep as a well
which breathed out warm air in winter like something asleep

subway-kiosk.proper: the subway kiosk outside the savings bank at {street} and {avenue}
epithets: outside a savings bank with columns, so the subway looked underdressed
where the gum wrappers blew round in circles on the landing
with a stair rail rubbed silver by a million palms

subway-kiosk.proper: the downtown kiosk at {street} and {avenue}, by the chestnut roaster
epithets: beside a chestnut roaster who kept his fire going for the smell as much as the trade
where the tiles on the stair were cracked in the shape of Italy
with a draught up the stairs that tasted of iron

subway-kiosk.proper: the Lenox Avenue subway entrance at West 135th Street
epithets: where all of Harlem came up out of the ground on its way home
with a kiosk painted green and a stairway always half full
where the shoeshine men worked the top step like a stage

subway-kiosk.proper: the subway kiosk at Astor Place
epithets: with beavers set into the tiles downstairs, in honour of a fur fortune
where the students from Cooper Union argued on the stairs
beside a traffic island where everybody crossed the wrong way

side-chapel.proper: the side chapel at St. Malachy’s on {street}
epithets: where the actors came to pray for good reviews
that smelled of wax and old stone and a little of greasepaint
with a rack of candles burning for causes nobody wrote down

side-chapel.proper: the side chapel at St. Brigid’s on {street}
epithets: built by men off the famine ships and still a little hungry-looking
where the kneelers had been worn thin by grandmothers
with a stained-glass saint who looked like she would rather be elsewhere

side-chapel.proper: the side chapel at Our Lady of Sorrows on {street}
epithets: a church whose name set the mood for the whole block
where the old women said the rosary in Italian and at great speed
that smelled of lilies and candle smoke

side-chapel.proper: the side chapel at St. Aloysius on {avenue}, the church with the copper spire
epithets: under a copper spire gone as green as a lime
where the candles were a penny and the prayers were free
with pews so old they creaked like a ship

side-chapel.proper: the little side chapel at St. Paul’s Lutheran on {street}
epithets: plain as a scrubbed table, the way Lutherans liked it
where last Sunday’s hymn numbers were still up on the board
that smelled of floor soap and hymn books

side-chapel.proper: the side chapel at the Church of the Transfiguration on {street}, which the block called the Little Church
epithets: which the block loved like a favourite aunt
with a little roofed gate and a garden no bigger than a rug
where more people got married in a hurry than anywhere else in the city

side-chapel.proper: the side chapel at St. Cecilia’s on {avenue}
epithets: dedicated to the patron saint of musicians, so the organ was held to a high standard
under a painted ceiling of angels who all seemed to have somewhere to be
where the candle rack held more stubs than candles

union-hall.proper: the union hall over Hoffmann’s bakery on {street}
epithets: up an outside stair that smelled of bread hours after the ovens went cold
where the folding chairs leaned in stacks against the wall like tired men
with a lectern pounded on so often it leaned

union-hall.proper: the garment workers’ hall over the Star Bakery on {avenue}
epithets: under a banner in Yiddish, Italian and English, all saying roughly the same thing
where the steam from the bakery came up through the floor and fogged the windows
that smelled of rye bread and strong opinions

union-hall.proper: the dockworkers’ union hall over Kearney’s bakery on {street}
epithets: where the chairs were built for big men and still complained
with a hand-lettered sign on the door about dues, underlined three times
where the coffee urn at the back had been on the boil since the last strike

union-hall.proper: the drivers’ union hall over Rosen’s bakery on {avenue}
epithets: over a bakery whose trucks the members drove, which made for lively meetings
with a portrait of the union’s founder glaring at the empty chairs
where every chair had a name carved in it and none of them matched

union-hall.proper: the bakers’ union hall over Schulz’s bakery on {street}
epithets: over the bakery, which saved the bakers a trip and gave them the smell to argue in
where the flour dust got into the meeting notes
with long tables that had been doors in a previous life

union-hall.proper: Liberty Hall, over the Vienna Bakery on {avenue}
epithets: named for liberty and furnished for thrift
with a stage just big enough for one speaker and his temper
where the posters on the walls were layered so thick the room was an inch smaller

union-hall.proper: the carpenters’ union hall over Vitello’s bakery on {street}
epithets: where the carpenters had built the platform themselves and it showed, in a good way
over a bakery whose cannoli came to every meeting uninvited
with sawdust in the corners that nobody could explain
